blocks.x: This is Roy Palmer speaking, and I want to say about the bands, different bands that we have played with in the Orleans and in different towns, different places. I want to explain how I came along in the music game. It was when I was around 15 or 18, I studied music, taking music. From that time I was taking bands, taking bands. I played with regular, and sometimes I played with other bands. I led a lot of bands, bass band and so on. My music was well established because I played and I played with other bands. I played with other bands. I played with other bands. I have an uncle who was a very good musician. That's the thing that caused me to take up music because he used to have a band playing. I was small. I was still very young. I was not a big fan of music. I was not a big fan of music. I was not a big fan of music. I was taking up from what I'd seen him do. I didn't know the instrument, couldn't play the instrument at that time, but this is what I thought. stuff Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. And we had several good trombone players. We always used sometimes two trombones in the chorus, you know, see we played together. And we'd used two trombones. And the fellow who played the seventh trombone, he would play baritones sometimes in the orchestra. We also had a very good banjo player. He was nice on banjo. And that was Johnny Cencere. He's from New Orleans also. Who was the clarinetist? The clarinetist was this fellow, Dewey, Lawrence Dewey. He played a C clarinet. And he was very good. He's still down there. Somebody's not going up. That's right. That's right. He's still down there. Well, was Louie Kepard, that's Freddie Kepard's name. Yeah, Louie Kepard. He was the fellow that played a guitar. He played guitar. He was a guitar player. And I don't know whether he changed or anything else, but that's what he usually featured, guitar. And we had several other musicians that came along the line, you know, at that time. Who was your drummer when you came up with? The drummer that we came up with, came here with, was a fellow by the name of Mack. A really young fellow. He must have been about eighteen, fifteen years old. Eighteen. Was it Mack Murray, was it? I don't know his last name, but I know his name was Mack. Yeah, Mack. He was very good, nice drum player. And we used so many different, you know, in the band, we'd use different musicians. At times some fellas wanted to play a gig, some nights would take a different fella, you know, and use them. And use the second trombone. And use the second trombone. I'd use this fella, well John Lindsay was one of the fellas. John Lindsay, he was one of the fellas, and he played with us several times, and two trombones. And George Fields, I played with them. There was, there was, there was first and second trombone. Any place where they had a very large orchestra, they'd use trombone two, two trombones. And these two trombones, one would play first and one would play second. And from that on, in Chicago, we began to build up a nice orchestra, or had nice musicians, or even had the girl playing with us from Chicago. And that was Lily Armstrong, the girl that married Lewis. So we had her playing with us a long while. And afterwards, Joe Oliver came in, and he started his orchestra, and we left the place where we was playing. We were at Dreamlin. And we left the Dreamlin, and we come over to Royal Garden, where, after we stopped playing there, where some of us quit the jobs, and some went one way in different places, you know, went in different directions, different bands, and joined, and that tore the band up. Okay, it's good one again. Tell me about the early days in New Orleans. Well, the early days in New Orleans, we usually played, we had lots of jobs to play through the weekdays, such as funerals and things like that, parties and picnics and other things we'd play, you know. If we'd get out too early, we'd never play it until in the evenings. We'd start around about seven o'clock, and dance or whatever we were playing before would be over with at twelve o'clock. They'd never run any further than twelve or one o'clock at the ladies. They'd let them go sometimes, but they never went over twelve o'clock. They'd start parties and dance. They'd go to the lawn parties and the lawn parties. Usually they do a lot of that work, the lawn party, giving dances out in the open air. What were they like? Well, you have a, it's a large space that they have surrounded with a large high fence, and they use it as a lawn ground for, you know, to dance on a nice lawn, and they'd give a party. They'd give it that way, and the dances would usually be about, there would be about maybe a hundred or two hundred people, you know, in this dance, and it was very good. Did they dance right on the ground? No, they had a pavement. They had a pavement. Some of them had wooden platforms they made, and they used to dance on that. And a good many, lots of times, we played dances on the pavements, you know, but they usually, people didn't go for those dances on the pavement much because they wore out the excuse, and so they usually go for a dance where canvas was laid or wooden floor. And we had a good many bands we played with, such as Tuxedo, Tuxedo Band was very good, Sonny Silistan, he died, but he was very good, and he had a nice band. And the Onward Band, that was good, those brass bands, and they played. Who was in the Onward Band? The Onward Band, George Fields, Manuel Mineta, Manuel Poe, and Ho Johnson, and Hank Johnson, and some of the old timers, you see. And they were very good, they were very good. They had a band that you might say stood up with any band, most of any other band. Most of my playing was with that band, and with the Tuxedo Band, and I used to go out of town and play with other bands, they'd hire me to play. I was supposed to be very good. I was supposed to be very good. So they'd hire me and they'd come and get me, you know, see, and bring me to those places where we had to play. And they'd bring me back home, see. And I had a pretty easy time in the music line. And I arranged a little. Did you do any teaching in New Orleans? Very little, very little I did, because I didn't have time to, from the time after I got in a certain height in the music, that I was able to give instruction and teach, I left, see. I didn't have to leave, but I left because I wanted to make a little money, you know, see. And in that ground, and in that field, they wasn't paying as much money as they played up this way, see. And I just come on up and got my bunch together and we started playing here. Now the first job we played here, it was on the circuit, you might say, the New Orleans Jazz Band, was playing from different theaters, different places. You know, we went to St. Louis, we went to Peoria, and all up Rock Island, and all those big theaters. We had an act, see, you had a small act, you had one woman and one man. And the rest of us, this. And Mabel Elaine, Mabel Elaine, Mabel Elaine was the girl that was on the show, see. She played a, she used a, played a, what do you call it? She played a comedian part, see. She sang there? She sang there, she sang. And we played on the, on the show. Then we went from there to St. Louis, and different places, Rock Island, Highway, and all, all different short trips, not too long, not too far away. We was working for Locales and Krause then at that time, Lee Krause and Mitchell Locales. They used to have the Broadway theater, at Broadway and 4200 Broadway. There was a theater over there. In Chicago? Yeah, in Chicago. They used to have that, they had that theater in charge. And most of our playing we did was, when we hung up, we stopped there and played there, and then we stayed around Chicago until we got another thing. You mentioned the Raleans, they didn't pay much. What did they, used to pay the dance? They run around about three or four dollars. They wasn't paying so much at night, see. At that time the scale was low anyway, see. And we didn't make so much. Some, some musicians made more, but they had a, you might say,

a very good band. What did they pay in the parades? In the parades they paid two dollars an hour. Yes, two dollars an hour. They only paraded about two hours and a half. We only made about four or five hours on the parade. We had so many different, and then through Connerville, and like those days, well we got hired. We had to play probably six or eight hours we played, see? Or eight or ten hours at night, see? For dances? Yeah, for dances, see? Different places at the fairground and at the Louisiana Park, and different places they had. On big nights like that, there's so many observers giving something, you know, dances, and so they'd hire different bands. But they'd use the best bands that they could get, see? Did you ever hear Buddy Bowling? Buddy Bowling? Yes, I did hear Buddy Bowling. He was a man that really, he was tough on trumpet, but he didn't play the trumpet like, like the phone. He started again about Buddy Bowling. Okay, and Buddy Bowling was one of the fellas he had, he was really a loud trumpet player, one of the loudest you ever was. You could hear him from here to the lake. He was very good, and the numbers that he played, he was, you might say he was used to those numbers, and he only played those numbers. He only played two or four numbers that he was more familiar with. He never played too many different numbers. And they all had their own tunes. They played their own music, their own tunes, and their own breaks. They used up their cells, you know, Buddy Bowling was very good though. Sonny Celestan, he was extra good. He was the true band leader too.
I've heard Celestan several times as band the last few years. Yeah.

Until he died just last December. Yeah, last December they say. And he was very good. He was good. And drummers, coming back to drums. Who was one of the best drummers in the last year? I think Baby Dots is one of the best drummers I ever played with. He gave me more time, a better time, twofold, than any drummer that I played with. See, I played with several drummers. Toby Hall is good too, see. And a minor. But Baby Dots is heavy and strong. Regular, you know. If you lose time on anything that you play in it, it's not his fault because he gives you very strict time. And he's very good. Do you remember any old time drummers like Louis Cantrell? Yeah, Louis Cantrell. He was very good. He used to play with an orchestra, one of the best orchestras around New Orleans. He was very, very good. Who's orchestra? He used to play with Robichaud, Robichaud's orchestra. They were very good. They got many dances for mostly. There was parties and there was 400 bunches. They played mostly for them. Did you ever play with Mac Murray? Mac Murray? I played with Mac Murray once or twice.
Maybe you can tell me this. Nobody ever seems to know how it spells name. Was his first name Mac and his last name Murray?

Yeah, I couldn't say M-A-C. M-A-C. M-U-R-R-Y. Is it all one name? What was his first name? They called him Mac, see. Mac was maybe his first name. But his name altogether. I think it was Mac Murray, see. That was his name, Mac Murray. All together, see. Yeah. His first name. His first name. I don't just remember what, but they'd call him Mac, anyway. Mac. Mac. Okay. Yeah. He was, hey, pardon. Did you play with Henry Zeno once or twice? Yeah. I played with him. Pop Foster. And he had a brother, Willie Foster, played the violin. We started an orchestra together. We, Pop Foster, Willie Foster, and a couple of other guys, new guys. And I didn't know they lived in the other part of town, you know, a French part of town. But we all got together and we had a very nice orchestra.
Pop said there was something called the Rocell Band or something. Do you remember that name? Rocells? I don't know. I didn't get the name right.
Yeah. Rocells had a good band. Rocells? Yeah. Rocells. Yeah. Rocells. They had a very good band. Was that the name of the musician? Rocells. Yeah. That was the name of the musician.
And Pop Foster said something about Joe Johnson, the trumpet player.

Yeah. He died. I didn't know much about that. Yeah. You wouldn't give him a new name because he died rather young. Joe Johnson. But he was hot. He was good. He was one who brought this trumpet playing like these fellas play now, see? And he picked that up from Joe Oliver. He lied under those fellas. And he followed their system. Kept up with their system. And he played trumpet just like those fellas. Well, what part of town did you come from? Up town? Up town. Up town.
Yeah. You remember about where you were born and raised? What?

No. Around the streets? Around up around Palmer's Avenue. My street. Palmer's Avenue. Howard. That's where I lived at. That's where I lived at. Was it named after some of your folks? Sure enough. No. It was named after another man. He was a doctor. Old doctor. And they named after him.
What other streets? I don't even remember that street. Up in Carlton. That's where up in Carlton.

Down in French, part of town. Around Perdita Street. I know you know those places. That's by Larry Armstrong. Yeah, Larry Armstrong. And Perdita and Rampard, different band. Bob Lyons and oh, I guess Frankie Deucin and all those guys. That was E-ball. Yeah, he played Trumbull. He was good. Very good. Tell me some more about your teachers. Oh, yeah. Now, a fellow that mostly, I got instruction from after my uncle died. I got from a fellow by the name of Jim Humphrey. Jim Humphrey. He had three or four sons. They're always musicians. Well, they're still living. And Willie, Willie, that's right. Yeah, uh-huh. Percy, a trumpet player. Yeah, that's right. I guess Earl Humphrey's dead. He's dead. He's been dead for years. 20 years. And there's one of them played clarinet. That was Willie. Willie. He's still playing. Yeah, yeah. And the old, old, old guy that his dad is named Willie too. I guess he's still playing Willie Humphrey. So I got good instruction from those fellows. And there was a fellow. Your teacher then is Willie? Jim Humphrey. Jim. Jim Humphrey. Yeah. And Frank Welch. Frank Welch was the man who taught me arranging and writing music. He wrote some of the most beautiful notes on a paper that you ever see. And I don't see how he could do it. He used to doctor with his ink, doctor his ink up with something that caused it to just stand right up. It wouldn't block, you know. And he taught me different phrases and how to keep out the other fellow's way, playing and playing a melody, you know, never get into the other fellow's melody. And he showed me how to, you know, keep in tone. He gave me instruction on the chords and how to form a chord, and what instrument could take the chord, and what instrument wouldn't take it, see. And he was a very good teacher. Very good. I had two, about two or three teachers that I went under. He was very good. Nice. There was kind, you know. There was kind fellows. And that way, if you've got a good, kind teacher, you can learn more, because he'll encourage, you see.
Mr. Welch, what was his first name?
That's Frank Welch.
What did he play? Any certain instrument better than others?
He played trumpet. He was a trumpet player. That's right. And a music arranger, beautiful music arranger.
When you started your very first lessons, did you learn to read music?
Yeah, with him. With him.
Your very first? Music that I started. Yeah. Did you start your music?

Yeah, he started me off in arranging and writing music, see. I heard my uncle play it several times, but I was too small to, you know, to take it up, see. But it seems like it stayed in my ear. Was that the first music you remember hearing, or the bands on the streets? Yeah, voice music, and then the bands on the street. That's the first music I began. Then I began to take an instrument, and after I learned scales and different things about the bands on the street, I began to learn, and then I played a little on violin and different instruments. And that's how I become familiar, more familiar with arranging than I did, see, because I was always mixed up with all the instruments. That's why when you hear me play trombone, I jump into somebody's part, but I sweeten it, see. That is make a nice melody to go in with that fellow that's playing. See, the average trombones, they play trombone, but they just play what they see, see. That is the music, they play just what they see. But if you know your chords and your phrases, you can play what you see, and then put more into it, see. In other words, improvise, see.
When you started, you started right on the trombone, was it very interesting? Yeah, on the trombone. How did you happen to like that better than others?

I don't know, I take my liking to trombone. There was a show that came into New Orleans, and they had two trombones. And I noticed a fellow that was playing trombone. He was quick and fast, and he could handle that trombone faster. Well, when I first started, I told fellows I was going to imitate that fellow. And they tried to disgust me. They said, you'll never play like that fellow. They said, you'll never play like that fellow. I said, well, I don't know, I'm going to try. And I kept trying and doing it wrong. You know, hard scales and minor scales and learning how to produce those tones, you know. I finally got it. I don't know, I just feel like since I heard that, I feel like grabbing up a trombone. What kind of a show was it? It was a circus. Oh, a circus? Yeah, it was a circus that came in. Circus come every September. See, every September. And the circus come around Christmas, December. And they come in town, and they bring those fellows. And they had one colored band, and they had two white bands. And that side show had these trombone players. And they really was good. They worked together, you know, harmonized. And I said from that, I said, well, I'll watch those fellows. And when I start to play them, I know just what to do, you know. And after I got through, I could play, and I met one of the fellows. He said, shucks. He said, I wish I could play like you. No. He wouldn't know if I had to do it. I said, I don't know why. I said, I paid attention to playing. Did you ever get their names of any of those? One fellow's named George Williams. He's one of the best supposed to be. He said that, I said that he was a better trombone player than I am, but he said I was better than him. So I, oh, he was wonderful.
There was one of George Williams that played in Handy up in Memphis.

Yeah. That's the same fellow, yeah. He's wonderful. He could do more with a trombone, I don't know, backwards, you know what you could say. I would play forwards, see. I practiced all that, but I never used it much, you know, but I knew it, you know. Practicing how you can find these trombone players now, they don't use backwards, you know, like that. All they know is what, forward, back, like that. But not playing back down, going down this way, they don't know nothing about that. Didn't that string? Lower position. Yeah, lower position. Make the scale right in the lower position. Keep down to your seventh position, but they never used it, see. I think that's why it's come so easier to me, too, to make all those different moves, you know, on trombone, because I played both positions, see. Played in lower position and forward, too, see.
Did you ever use pedal tones much on trombone?
Oh, yes, I had a good ambusho. At one time, I could hit the highest note and drop down below, below the ground.
I used to practice that, see, because that's what they used to have said.

Oh, you can make high notes, but you can't make no low notes. And some father said, well, you can make low notes, and you can't make no high, see. So I fought hard to get both, see. And sometimes I would catch myself and be playing a melody or something like that, and make that high note and drop down. And I noticed that, you know. I'd say, no, that's easier to do. If you get the ambusho for it, you know, you can do it just, look like, without the least effort, see. We played a dance once. We played a dance over in, uh, Streeter. You know, Streeter, Illinois. Yeah. And there was a high school band that was playing there. We was playing. I was playing with a fellow by the name of Oscar Young. We played over there in the park. They give us some nice park, the band, the brass band was playing over on one side, and we was playing on the other side. Before we got through playing the man, the professor had them all the way watching me. I said, what the world of them guys? They're watching you, see.
I said, well, I'll just go to the ground.
go ahead now and try not to make too many mistakes.

Because he was listening. They're teachers. This man was teaching these young fellas, and they had a big band. And he was telling them, I could see him telling them something. I don't know what he was telling them. He was telling them something. And they stood there, and those guys stayed right around me. I kind of felt embarrassed, you know. But they never heard the trombone thing. That was the trombone they ever heard. So that was one of my attempts to find out whether I was good or not. And after we come back in Chicago, we played at Deluxe. The upstairs had a, what do you call it? Taverns then? Yeah. We played up there. Was that on State Street? On State and 35th. There was a fellow come from the Army. He'd come in. First man he started picking there was me. Where did you get this guy? I said, he's tough. He said, what's, what's your, how long have you been playing? I said, oh, just a couple of months. He said, you can't fool me with that. He said, you don't need to think you're fooling me with that. He said, I'm a trombone player myself. I didn't say no more. Well, you see, it's something, I don't know, it's something different. I'm not saying bragging on my trombone playing, but it's something different because when I play around places, before I get through, the whole gang is right up there in front of me. And the other fellas, they ain't paying so much attention, but they're watching me, see. And we had, we had a very good band. This Paul Barberine, he played with us for a while. I know him. He's a nice little drummer. And he didn't stay in Chicago long. He only stayed a while. But he was very good. But Baby Dots is just about as good a drummer as a man wants for strict time. Yeah, I think so. Yeah, he's as good a drummer as a man wants. He'll hold a time. Time. He gets a tempo. He's got it. All those boys that played, there was none of them that I could play with. You know, I played all of them, but they're so easy to play with Dots. I think he played with you with Hightower's band
back in New Orleans.
His first job,
his first professional job.

That's right. Charlie Fewclose. Charlie Fewclose. Yeah. Uh-huh, yeah. George Fewclose. George. George Fewclose. Who else was in that band? Oh, we had some boys instruments. Okay. Okay. The instruments they use now, trumpets and trombones and so on, the most they use now is a shallow mouthpiece. Not so deep, a shallow mouthpiece. They're made special for high notes, see? And when you have high notes to make, it's easy with those mouthpieces. It produces a high tone, and you have to figure out, you have to work away, you got to work with an ambush show to get a low note. But they're easy for high notes, just like that. What kind of mouthpiece do you recommend? I recommend a medium mouthpiece. It's not too deep and not too shallow, see? It's just medium bowl, see? That's the best, that's the best, because you make yourself, see? And that way, you got your, you have the abilities to make what you want to make, and you don't have to have too much help, see? When this mouthpiece is made shallow, this mouthpiece helps you to make high notes, see? And low notes, you got to scramble, see? You have to scramble for low notes on shallow mouthpiece. But when you get one that's a medium mouthpiece, you can get high in both low and high. So you're very good. What make horn did you use? Are there any certain kind of horn? I use a corn horn. I use CG corn, and I use yoke, and, uh, well, here's when I first started, a little American system, a little cheap horn, you know, trombone, until I began to learn good, and after I got better instruments, see, I was able to have money to get me a good instrument, but first time, I took the, the cheap instrument. Is there any particular brand you like better than the other? Well, I liked, uh, King. That was a good trombone. King trombone is one of the, one of the best trombones. And corn is very good and nice, but King was better. It had a bigger bow, you know, and you could just run up them high notes and drop down. You notice me on that, uh, that was a King trombone I had, see. Just get them low notes so easy and come out so nice, you know, and smooth. You couldn't blast it, see. It never, you never blast a King instrument, not those trombones, because they had a large bow, see. And when you made high notes, they come up so sweet and nice, you know, up there. So that's why I like, uh, King, King trombone. Tell me about
the bell on the trombones. I don't know much
about these things.
Yeah. Nowadays, they try to get great big bells. Big bells, yeah.

Does that change the tone? Yes, it do. It makes a, makes a sharp tone. It's like the trumpets, see. These trumpets, they make, now, with little bells. Them trumpets, they make, with small bells, is a piercing tone, you know. It's, it's, I don't think it's so good with those, and even with trombones. Not so, such a big bell, but a medium. We call it seven-inch bell. That's the best trombone to get. Seven-inch bells, seven-inch bell. And you get too much bell, it, it, it, it stays right around a bunch and you can, you don't go out, see. And people sitting out, and they're listening at a band, they want to hear all of the instruments, see. And sometimes with a big bell like that, you don't hear the, you don't hear the trombone at all. That sometimes when you got nice, sweet little notes to make, you can't get it. And the big bell,
you hear it more like

that? Big bell right in the band, all the hip, you can't hear yourself from right up under, but when you get way out there, see, that's what you got to hear. The trombones today, I noticed most of them have these little weights back there. Yeah, weights back there. They didn't used to do that,
did they?
I think that was a good system now that they got because, that thing's gone down now, but when I play trombone, that thing goes big,
big right in there,
right there where I help
the trombone,
right on there, that's it,
on the second finger. Just holding it up. Yeah,
that weight, see, by getting up, when I got one with the weight to it, that balanced it back off of my finger and I could play much easier to it. This way, I had to hold it up. You said trombone
doesn't rest on your shoulder or anything.

I used to rest mine. I used to rest mine. Some people didn't like to rest them on their shoulder. A lot of fellas, because they dirty, they collar. But I used to rest mine on my shoulder, you know, and when I felt like raising it up, I'd take it up. Yeah, raise it up.
Is there anything, advice you had, like some trombones always hold it way up in the air and you try to play? I never got to see you that way.

I think the best way for a trombone to hold is trombone straight in front of them and just a little up, like you was telling me about holding my head for that picture. Not too high, see, but just a little up. That makes the sound go right over their heads of the people's dance and like that. Not too high, because it's going up to the ceiling.
Just a little bit more than straight out.
That's right, more than straight out. That's right. You always could blend with them, see.
Did they always use oil in the old days for sliding? The trumpet players have to spit on the valve, you know?

Yeah, well, I used to use, I used oil too, but oil, it kept us buying so expensive in a way. You had to be buying but 25 cents a bottle, but you would use it, yeah, see. What I did, I used kitty-kill sale. Kitty-kill sale. Just take the kitty-kill sale and throw it on your slide all the way down, grease your slides good, and after you grease your slides with this kitty-kill sale, you put a little kerosene on it, and that slide will fly. And it doesn't evaporate as fast? No, it doesn't evaporate as fast. But they haven't used Vaseline, or is that too stiff? It is too stiff. A lot of fellas used it, but it's hard dragging. I tried it once, but I couldn't, couldn't get away at all. See, it's just stiff, hold your hand. Anything else about the care of instruments? Well, the care of instruments should be always, it should be mopped out after any engagement that you play. You should take that instrument and mop it out. You'd have one of those long rods and run it through there. Go through the slides and everything? Yeah, through the slides and through the other part. See, that is, you wouldn't go, you have to take it off. you had a long rod with a little bit of flesh rag on it or some kind of a, you might say, a woolen cloth on the end. And you carry it through the slides on the outside and sometimes you push out dirt, like dirt. You know, that's when your slide working, it throws that grease down and it goes in there. You push that out. Well,
I used to see, Buck Johnson and I used to record him, sometimes he would run water through his trombone under a faucet.
Yeah, well, that's a good way to it. It keeps the instrument moist, see, yeah.
Did you ever wash out your trombone that way too? No,

I'd wash my horn when I'd get through playing. I'd use hot water and soap to wash my horn but as long as I'm playing I go back to play. Then I run it on the end of the system, you know, that's to dampen it up because the horn doesn't sound so good dry. You'll notice that when a fellow picks up a horn and it's dry, he can't get nothing much, but as soon as you pull that water in it and it softens, it seems like it softens the metal or something and you'll get easy tones out of it. And that's what I used to, that's the way I used to play.
I was going to ask about your embouchure, any certain exercises, did you practice long notes or any certain kind of...

Well, the best way to practice to get a good embouchure is play the lowest notes you can get on it and then play the high notes, you know, play the lowest note and play a pedal note and see how long can you hold that pedal note. Hold that pedal note as long as you can hold it, see, and then after you hold that pedal note and go up in the middle register and go up on the high register and when you get through during that, you're tough.
When you started, how long would you practice? How long would you advise the people?

I used to practice sometimes two and three hours just depending on how, you know, that's why I imagined it helped me a lot, see, I practiced two and three hours just, I didn't have anything to do, you know, and I just went on and practiced two or three hours. Every day? Every day I practiced two or three hours, see, that's why I could do anything I want with the trombone. I didn't care what, you know, you had to do with it, I could do the same thing with it. I seen a fellow that, he was downtown in the loop and he played two tones on the trombone and I thought that that was, I thought that it was hard, which it was hard after you learned how to lift the instrument, you know, two tones on the trombone playing the lead and playing the alto, two, see. Two tones at the same time? Two tones at the same time. So I kept his lip to vibrate two different notes. Yeah, to vibrate two different notes. And I studied it for a long time. I got it down pretty good. You could do that? Yeah, see, I got it down pretty good, two tones. It sounded like two trombones. It'd be one, but the way you'd hold your lip, it'd carry a vibration with the other tones. When you played that,
did you go up like in thirds? Yeah, I'd go up in thirds. You couldn't go down on one and up on the other. No, no, no. You both would go up together. They would go up together.
They would keep close together in thirds. Yeah, something like that. I worked nice to it. Yeah, there's a good thing
about to do that.

No? I had a fellow here named Augustine. He was a trombone player. He come from Memphis. He was one of the first I saw after I saw this fellow do it downtown, the loop. But it's easy. You can't press your loop too hard. Just let it loose, see, and practice getting your note what you're going to start on and then let your loop loose and then that third comes right in, see, follows it up. I had a lot of experience on those things,

see. What about pressure? For a while, it was a fad they use, as they say, no pressure at all. I've seen people in the demonstration of a trumpet hanging up on a string and walked up to it without touching it and hit a high C without any pressure. Without any pressure. Yes, I don't know what I'm saying.

Well, that's pretty good, but I'd rather play a whole and one trombone, see, because you can handle it. Of course, you can handle it just as well in terms of professionals too, but I'd practice holding one trombone because there's a certain way you can hold the trombone and not bear it too hard and not let it too loose. See, some fathers play with a loose pressure, see, and some players have got to hold it all hard up against the left, but the way to do it is use medium pressure and that way you can handle it, you can do what you want in that mouthpiece, you know, make that horn do what you want, but if you've got it too tight, you might drop it and jump up to a high note, you can't do it, see, because you've got too much pressure on it, and you can't change the note like you want.

Is there any certain things you can tell about some trumpet players and trombones they wear out after a few years, they've hit this shot and they can't play anymore, is there any certain thing that, I imagine the way you play, when you play right, you can play forever, I should say. All the time, yeah. Is there anything you can tell about that?

Well, one thing I can see about it is those fellas that play that way, you know what does that? You know what kills the mouthpiece, you know what kills them on, they use too many mouthpieces. Some fellas, they'll use a mouthpiece tonight and tomorrow night he's got another mouthpiece, and they'll use another mouthpiece and they'll use

And then the next time you see him, he got another mock piece. You can't get used to a mock piece that way. You got to almost, that mock piece had to become a part of you almost, you know. If you lose a mock piece, you're in bad shape. That's why they changed too much, see. And you changed horns? Did you keep your same mock pieces? Kept it all. I wouldn't get rid of it for nothing. I kept it, yeah.
You don't have it?

Yeah, I still got it. So you see, you're changing mock pieces all, every time they play somewhere. Maybe they'll change, get another mock piece, and they'll change and get another one. And that's no good. Use the same mock piece. If you can get used to one, you can stay on that one. And the instrument, you get a different instrument, you can play it much easier, see, with the instrument.
But too many high notes, trying to strain for high notes, would that kill you?

That's a bad thing. That's a bad thing. But you see now, the way it is now, the way the mouse piece is manufactured, they're shallow, and they can get those high notes. So they don't have to strain. No, they don't have to strain to get them. The only scrambling they have to do is when they have to go down to low notes. You notice, you watch those fellas.
Yeah, that's a fella.

You notice when they're playing down in the low notes, they play all the high notes, but when they come down, it sounds like metallic. You know, you get a metallic sound. It's because it can't get on there like you want. Not with low notes with a shallow mouthpiece. Mouthpiece will be medium. See, and then when you've got a medium mouthpiece, not too shallow and neither too deep. Just medium, and you can play in that mouthpiece all day and all night. You don't have to worry. See, it don't hurt you. But you've got a shallow mouthpiece. You play in high notes, and then you want to get on to the low notes, and you can't do it. You can't do it. It's saved your life. You can do it, but sometimes you get used to it and can't play them, but those pedal notes and those low notes, it's cracked. You know, you can't get them out like they want.
Are there any good books on trombone? Do you remember the book you started with? Yeah.
Yeah, I used to, Ben Verricon. That was one of the first books I got, Ben Verricon.
Ben Verricon.
Ben Verricon, yeah. I think they still got those books, yeah.
Ben Verricon. Published by Carl Fisher. Yeah, yeah, that's right. When you started on trombone, you remember the book that your uncle gave you or anything?
Yeah, I can't think of the name. Now, let's see. His name is a book now. I'll give this boy one. He's good. A trumpet? Yeah. I can't think of that mouthpiece. That book.
That's Arbonne.
That's it. I think that's it.
That's a trombone.
Yeah, they got everything now. Arbonne. That's the book I gave him. Oh, he's nice. You should hear him play.

Well, when you started, did you, I know Bunk tells about when he started on trumpet. He studied at school and had a Mexican teacher and made him study solfetch. Yes, yes. The sight reading. Yes, sight reading. Did you have to go through that before you took up your instrument? Or how did you think?

Well, it seemed like to me that, I don't know, the man said that it was natural for me. See? Because I have a large lip and I played in a large mouthpiece. And he said it was natural for me that I didn't have the words. And he told me, he said, you're going to come to be one of the best trombone players of tears. I didn't think he'd do it. I just played just to, you know. Yeah, he could tell. Make a little air. He could tell, you know, from the way I handled the instrument. He said, you'll be one of the best of tears. But I didn't play that no more. I tell fellas, not. He's another fella, too. There's a fella by the name of Zoo Robertson. I didn't talk about him.
You were talking about Zoo Robertson? Zoo Robertson, yeah.

He was the only man, he was one of the best fellas that would go with me in bands, playing those brass band jobs, you know, like that. We played together all the time. He played first and I played second. He played on one side and I played on the other. You know, in fumes and like that. He was very good. Nice trombone player. Sweet, you know. Not a lot of harshness. He just played nice and sweet. When he had to play loud, well, he could play loud. But he always played. We'd practice that together. I used to go to his house every day and he'd come to my house. And we'd practice like that.
Was he about the same age or a little older?

Yeah, he might have been a little older than me. Because he was a settled man. He was a man when I met him. He must have been about six or seven years older than I am. But he was good. Jack Carroll, my Carroll brothers.
I never met Jack.
He's a man who played the trombone. Never knew a note. He never worried about notes. He could play, but he never worried about notes. He mostly played his music by head.
I guess Zou was a good reader. Oh, yeah.
Zou was a nice reader. He could play a little bit of piano, too. Oh, that's right. He played later in theaters.
Yeah, he could play a little bit of piano. He and his wife, I believe, traveled.
Yeah. Is that her name? Jessie?

What was the name of it? Once, I remember, even in the Defender. Wife, remember what? Had a wife and she played piano in Oregon, too. They had a job in some theater going around the country. And for a while were in West Virginia once, playing in the theater.

Yeah, he was very, very good. Nice, John Mo. That's when he was only thing about him. He liked trombone correct and everything. But he wouldn't play with a fellow if he didn't play, you know, right. You know, a man come in and played with him, played double with him, and get to blast him.
Maybe that's why some people thought he was sort of mean. Yeah. Some children come in, right.
He wouldn't have a face of a strong. Yeah, he wouldn't have a word with him. We'd talk. So that's why they say he was kind of funny, you know.
Yeah.
Nice, trombone correct. Yeah, I worked with him several times. George Field was good.

Yeah, I didn't get to meet him. He died about two or three years ago. Yeah, George Field. I went to his house a couple of times here. Once talked to a niece. Uh-huh. He was over at the Union playing cards that afternoon. Yeah. Before I ever got back, he was dead then. Yeah. He was very good.

Very good. Nice trombone player. I used to see him play in marches. I was rather young then when he used to play in those bands, you know. Before I got down with bands, I saw him playing in that. And they'd play marches, you know, and things like that. He was a nice trombone player. That's what I learned. And I found out that playing trombone, when you're playing and making those smears, you know, and te-de-de-de-da-da, and following up to the other instrument, I paid attention to him, watched him closely on a lot of music he played. He was good. Oh, and Joe Petit.

Oh, yeah. Oh, Lord. One time I made a record of him, honey, was so old that he could hardly play. He played the sound without any teeth, no false teeth. He played both? He played just on the ground, not so well. No. The trouble was this. He was quite deaf. He could hardly hear. And one number they started out, he couldn't even hear what key they were playing in. Oh, I see. He started in the wrong key. Then when he found out what key it was, he heard it finally and changed. Yeah. But he made a couple of numbers just to see how he would sound. Nothing I was ever going to issue, but that was 1944, 1945. Oh, yeah. Joe Petit. And he played Careless Love and St. Louis Blues. When he was young, I guess he used the valve trombone. Yeah, that's right.
That's what he used to hear.
But he used slide when he...

Joe Petit was a fellow for him. He had a good tone, too, on trombone. And they had another fellow that I played with, Joe Petit, named Yank Johnson. That's Buddy Johnson's brother. That Yank had... They could put some of the powerfulest tones in the trombone. They didn't think about sweetness, you know, or nothing like that. They just blasted out. I mean, they could blast them, too. Too loud, you know. On a parade, it was all right. Yeah, in a parade, it was all right. But, you know, playing in a dance or in a place where a party was, you couldn't do that. You could do it, too, but the people didn't like it so well. You played nice and soft. The music is sweet, you know. We had a lot of boys, you see. I'm going to start telling them fellas how to play trombone. Because I listened to them covered in white. Some of them wouldn't do it on trombone. Some of them handle the instrument, all right. But, you know, they don't understand how to take advantage of it, see. They don't take advantage of it. They just blow, blow, blow. Now, I tell you, a fella plays a nice trombone. This fella, them two brothers, what is his name? They play downtown all the time. Here in town now? Tom and Darcy? That's it.
No, he plays a nice trombone. He plays pretty good. Yeah, he gets a pretty tone.
Yeah, he gets a nice tone. And his brother, the trumpet player, out there.
Or the clarinet jimmy.

Yeah, clarinet jimmy d'arcy. He plays a nice trombone. He's good. Don't have no whole lot of loud noise, you know, and all like that. I heard him play solo. I heard him play the number behind the band. And with the band, I heard him play the number. And he's good. Do most of the bands play too loud, do you think? Yeah, they could gauge themselves. They could gauge. You know, some fella won't argue. I won't argue you. I want to be seen. I want the people to see me playing better than you allowed. And you see. And I get up there and I ain't going to let you play your part right because I'm going to try to go over you and all that stuff. When they play together, then you'll find out. Nice.

In the New Orleans bands, I know some people told me how they used to work out things playing some parts soft. And then they do it right now. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And you talk over before, the leader will tell you how to do it.

Yeah, they come solo. Sometimes the leader, he'll just say, and they just quiet right down. See? Quiet right down. You don't have to tell them nothing. Just stop right away. They watch you and they go right down. Then when you want them to come up to me, of course, you make a motion. You want them to pick up the double-folder and then they go into it. See? But then when you want your soft, that's all you do it. And they come down. I mean, that's why a fellow asked me, he said, how do you know when they're going to get soft like that? If you're watching the leader, you can't help them. You tell yourself, you tell that, you've got to come down on you. Oh, there's lots of little tricks in the bands, you know.
Usually the trumpet player is the leader, but sometimes the trombonists and others, if you have any ideas on who should be the leader or why in New Orleans, if they usually have to come up.

I'll tell you about the bands. Like, I've seen tenor saxophones. I saw tenor saxophone lead a band. That is the leader of the band. He took the most principled parts, see, of what he had to do, of their work. He took the principled parts of it and he led the band. See, he had trumpet players there and he gave them their parts, you know, what they had to use. But he led the band off. Then it was a nice, sweet band. That's the trumpet, trumpet, tenor saxophone. Tenor saxophone, a nice instrument anyhow. Arnett Nelson used to play with us. We played at Rich Carlton. Oh, yeah, Cotty Grove and we played there. And Arnett played the tenor saxophone. We had Weatherford. You don't know what that is. He's dead now. He's not an Indian. Died there. He played with us. Weatherford, Arnett Nelson. And a boy named Harris, drum player. A boy named Willie Harris, I think his name. He played drums with us. And Tommy Latney, you never met him. Oh, yeah.
Sure, I knew him in New York. He died too, didn't he? Yes, 1939 he died. Yeah, Tommy Latney. I heard the last records he ever made. I got to go to this session. He made it for Victor.
I see.
With Mesro and Judy Singleton. Yeah. That's how it is.
And this guy Jackson, is he playing still? A.D. Jackson?
A.D. Jackson. A.D. Jackson. I know him. I taught him.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, not him. Just another Jackson. He played. I believe he played drum. I think he played drum. Jackson. He played. He went off from here with. He went off from here with. This guy, he has all the bands in charge. Most of Noble Sisson. He went off with Noble Sisson. And he was playing with them. He was a good drummer.
Sidney Bichet was with Noble Sisson.
Did you ever play with Sidney? Yeah, sure. Sidney come up right around me. He did. We played together several times. Sidney Bichet. He's nice too.

No, he's in Paris. He likes it in France. Yeah. He's been there. Did he have a wife? Did you take him? Yeah, he's had two wives since he was in Europe. I'm German. I'm rather old. Let me see. Somebody has seen Sidney recently. He came back from France and said he's married a real young girl now. Sidney Bichet.
He is a good clarinet player.

Yeah, I knew his brother very well too. A doctor. That's right. He died three years ago. Yeah. I always went to see him every time I go to New Orleans on vacation. He's having me there for dinner. Yeah. Offly nice. Yeah, Leonard was a nice guy. He played trombone. Yeah, he so did. He died, you say? Yes, he wasn't too good a musician. He was a doodest, wasn't he? He was a dentist. Yeah. He fixed up a cape for Sidney and he fixed up Bunk's ball, Steve. Bunk playing with ball, Steve. Yeah.
Had Dr. Bichet in there. Dr. Bichet. He's nice. He's a nice fellow. Leonard, I think his name was.
Yes, Leonard. When did you play for Sidney?

I played with Sidney before he left. He left here. I played a couple of jobs. Not here. He left New Orleans. And I played a couple of jobs with him. And he used to come. But that's where he got his start, right with us. We used to take him and let him play, you know.

and he had that style too, that Big Eye Louie style, that clarinet, and he'd come with us, we'd let him, he'd call that sitting in, let him sit in, you know. I was glad to sit in because he was catching on, you know, a lot of stuff, and he'd come over and play with us sometime, we'd let him sit in, and he had that system like Louie, Big Eye Louie, but he wasn't reading so much, you know.
They tell me Louie didn't read so much either.
Not in the beginning until he went on the boat, they said.
Then he really had to learn to read on the boat.

Did you ever play on any boats? I played a couple of jobs on a boat, but I didn't like it. I was afraid of the boats. I played a couple of dances on there. I remember even going up and down in the water, just thinking about that boat sinking.
I can't swim either. No, me either, I can't.
Me either, I can't. That's why I wouldn't bother a good job.
I was raised on Mississippi River Tree, a camp in Missouri, right over there, but I never liked to swim. Some of those boats used to come to our town.
I just wondered if I ever heard you, maybe didn't know you in the old days. Faith Malibu. Yeah. Faith Malibu, he's one of the fellow. There's another Faith, too, that's in California.
You might have met him, a tall, light fellow, played trombone.

I've heard that name. Faith, what is his name? I don't know whether he's going to see. Somebody played with... He played with Bill Johnson in them, too. I think he's played with Ice Can Tate, too. He played with Bill Johnson in them out there, I think, too. Really? I've never met him. Bill Johnson's been to California again, they tell me. I haven't seen Bill Johnson in the middle. Is he back now? Yeah, he's back now. I haven't got to see. He said a man can't get a job in California if he don't belong to that union. Yeah, that's true. He can't get a job. He can wait a while. Yeah, make you wait a while. You've got to be there a year before you can get a job, see? I told him, I said, you'll probably go to California and let him figure on going to work, and then after you get there a while, make yourself acquainted and then, you know, stay around. Yeah, so, yeah. Well, I'm surprised we were here about Eddie Gallen. I didn't know that. Yeah? I had to scrap with the oldie. And he's not hard to get along with, I don't believe. Oh, yeah. Everybody I know likes him.

He's such a friendly fellow. What is his address? I don't know for sure. I have it at home. I'll try to find it. Yeah? I'll make a note of it right now. Yeah. I have it at home. Unless he's moved. I haven't seen him for about six or seven years. I see. Well, he was supposed to come here this winter. There was one trumpet player, a white kid, who had a band. And when he left Ory, he was going to get him to come here in June. But Garland didn't come with him. Oh, I guess. Maybe June. Because he didn't want to travel. Yeah. So I'll look up his address. If I don't know it, this kid I know, this trumpet player could tell me where he lives. And some other friends I have out there, too. I see. He always looked well and looked as young. Like David said, there's nobody that's as young as you. How do you do it? Do you know it? Do you know it? Do you know it? Do you know it? Do you know it? Do you know it? Do you know it? Do you know it? He'll look just as young as I was 30 years old. I heard something in 1940. That's 50 years ago. Same thing.

What do you do? Well, take care of yourself. You know, man, don't run around too much and getting drunk, laying out in the snow. That ain't no good. No, that's true. I saw some nice musicians. I had to clap. It was a shame. You haven't lost your hair, no gray hair or anything? No. Well, that's just to keep up. See? I don't drink at all. I lost all of my hair. Well, some people do lose their hair early, you know. Yeah, that's right. And a lot of people just keep their hair a long time before they, you know, travel. Yeah, I never worry about nothing. But if you get to worry, you're going to get a whole inch over. I see fellows around my age out of the crowd. I just feel sorry for them.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, I feel sorry for them.
Well.

All of a sudden they go to pieces. Yeah, all to pieces. And it seems like they worry a lot, you know, about, you know, I used to worry about nothing. And eat plenty. Do like you and me. Get your food and have a nice meal. And don't run out and get drunk and all that stuff. Laying out in the snow. That's bad. Yeah, if you take care of yourself, it's better. That's the better, you know, because even so, man, I have a million years to live in. You just might as well enjoy it and take, you know, do the best of it you can, see. I didn't quit trombone, stop playing trombone because it was too hard for me or, you know, anything like that. The only thing I quit, it wasn't no work, Russell. No, that's right. It wasn't no work. I'd rather go to work than to do like a lot of those guys, get out and get to stealing and robbing and, you know.
Can you tell me about Freddie Keppard?
Did you play with him? He played with him. He played, he come with us at Deluxe. At not Deluxe, at Dream. And he played with us a while at Dream. That was a Dream one at 35th Street and State.
Yeah, that's right.

One out of West Harlem. Yeah, I sure was. And he played with us at Dream over here, see. And he was a good trumpet player. Nice trumpet player. He had one style of playing, though. He had jazz style, too, pretty good. But he didn't have it like so much of it as the other fellas, you know. He was very good, and he knew his instrument nice. And he put good tones in it. And that guy would get to playing sometimes and play in the melody and get to sweating. He was so fat, you know. Sweating? Yeah, he was so fat. By the time he started playing, he began to get sweating, you know. And Louis Armstrong does that, too, now, see. About six or eight handkerchiefs. He got to carry about eight handkerchiefs with him, see. I don't know. I don't know whether it's that beer or what it is, but whatever it is, they got it down, see. They used it with handkerchiefs, and mostly for sweating and getting my heart's in.
Here's another question. I keep changing the subject, but I think about it. Louis' neck puffs out so when he plays.
Did you ever have any trouble like that? No, I never did do that. And puffing the jaw.
Is there anything you can tell people?

I brought it from the throat, just right from the throat, right out of the throat. I never puffed my jaw. I don't know why they do that. Very seldom, very seldom I'd puff my jaw. Not on pedal, even on pedal notes, I wouldn't puff my jaw.
There's one trombonist there, George Brunus, a white fellow from New Orleans.

Oh, no, that boy, I know him. He just come from over in our jays. He come from across the river. We come up together on here. George Brunus and Milton Brunus, his brother. Yeah. And I forget this other boy. There was another boy come up here with an orchestra.
Paul Merez. Yeah, Paul Merez. Well, there was another trombonist down there, Tom Brown. Yeah, Tom Brown. Oh, he had a band.
He came up there pretty early. I remember him. I remember him.
Anyway, Brunus puffs out just one cheek. Just one cheek, yeah. Is he playing here? Yeah, he's up at the 11-11 Club at Bryn Mawr. Yeah? On the north side. He's been here for four years.

Another boy, too, was with them. I forget his name. He played trumpet. He quit playing, though. He's from downtown. What is that fellow's name? I couldn't think of a name. Jelliro knew them all. But Brunus is a raised trombone player, a puff boy. He's in jail like that.
Is there anything you can do about that?

Yeah, he's just laying off a trombone. He'd have to lay off trombone about two or three months and change the style of playing. I had a style of playing, too. And I changed that style. I saw it wasn't no good and it prevented me from making quick passages. You know, see? All that stops you. You see that wind. You got drawed back in there. And you're trying to execute with the instrument. It's very hard. A good trombone player, but they're lazy and slow. You know, they ain't got that snap, see? They can't do it, see? Because the jaw is full of wind. And they're trying to make quick passages. And that wind got to come way back up here.

Yeah, and go around, see? Is there anything you can tell about the style the trombone should play in a band that is more of a... I know some of this myself. I mean, I know how you play and how they sound. Yeah, sure. But anything that you could say here on the record, like whether it should be more of a bass part, or if they do pretty, they play cello parts. Yeah. Should it be more of a rhythm? Yeah. Or what kind of a melody?

Well, it depends on how the melody runs. If you've got a good stomp melody, you know, or something like that, trombone should be played right between the melody and the other part of the harmony, like the after beats and the after counts and all that. And you use, you might say, well, you might say a whole note. Use a whole note in some places, you know, see? And then use, play a figurations, you know, a figurations around, playing those figurations around on a melody when a fellow's playing. And don't stay in your part all the time. Jump in the lead somewhere else. Don't stay there long, though, because you're taking his part from him. Play hitting the lead sometime and get away from there and going back to vamping and bass. And that's the reason I could balance, make a, I could balance any orchestra. I could put any orchestra on good balance because that's the way I play with him, see? I'll play the lead around when the fellow thinks I'm moving my ducks away from him and go over here. I could hear it on the rest. See, you can hear it on the things. Duck away from him and go over there somewhere.
Is there a trombone that can play either melody or sort of like a rhythm part, too, at times?

Yeah, rhythm is. With little sharks to play, like you say, snap it off. Yeah, it snaps off, see? That's the peggos and things like that in the part. It's nice if you can handle them, see? A lot of fellas try to handle them and they get some mixed up, see? And it slows them down, see? It slows them down. You can't get those notes in between those peggos, you know? And that kind of slows them down. That's what makes them scared to take venture out, you know, to try to do anything. If you can play a peggos and you're, you know, with that peggos, you play it in and then jump into the melody. But some fellas, when they're doing that, making a peggos, they make it so slow, they can't get that up note, you know? They can't get that turn note, see? There's turns, you know, see? Like that. It's easy, all right.
When you play a solo, what do you try to do?

Well, sometimes I take a solo and when they're playing, they're vamping me, see? And I'm playing this solo. I may take it up in 16ths, see? I may take it up in 16ths, play a whole note and use some 16ths with it. But I'm going to use 16ths in the place of it, but with the same melody, see? Just like you say. I may go. See, I'm going on with the melody right on, but I'm putting something in between there, see? See? See, I get on back on that part. I never stay in that part. See, I go away from it, see. Because if you continue playing with him, with his melody, you know, I keep playing the melody, well, that takes the sweetness away from the beauty, away from the peace from him. See, he might have a nice part to play, see. Well, I'll start him off with it, see. Every boy to get in together, I start him right off with it, like, I'm going to stay with him, and after a while, I'm gone. They got a lot of little tricks in it, see, playing that way. And it helps the other fella, and a lot of fellas likes to take down, you know, when they're playing the melody and like that. Because all you got to do is just bow his head. If he's going to take down, he's losing the lead or something. Look over there at me, I'll hold him eight measures and play it for him, and then I'll turn him loose and go right on back into that part. Vamping on trombone is the best thing that a man could do. Vamping on trombone and playing an off melody. That sweetens the band right up, see. Playing if you're playing. Not all the way through, boom, boom, boom. You know, you heard them records some further. He couldn't go nowhere but vamp, vamp, vamp, vamp. And that's all he could do. By vamping, you mean just by. That's just vamping, you see, like that nine, and you play it, and then get away from it, see. You vamp it, get away from it, take some lead, see. And you're listening. That's when you're playing a piece, and you're playing it by music or by ear. Listen for the guy, what he's doing over there, see. Whatever he's doing over there, you do it different but do it in units, see, together. They say, that's a sweet band, sure. It's going to be sweet when they're all working together. And the guys used to point out to fellas, you know, who they want. Take the break. Take the break. Fellas stood up one night, about two hours, said, how do you fellas know when or who's going to take it? He don't know. See, even the leader just pointing over to the fella, you know. He don't know. He said, how did he know he had to take that break? He used to it. They got it down, see. And we used to play over at the place over here on Wells. And that's the first place we played when we come in Chicago.

Really? Mr. Tavern? Yeah, it was a tavern. Oh man, that place was like the idea of a band from York. That man made money, I mean he made money, hand over fist. He wanted to keep us, but I don't know, it seemed like them fellas that he had, you know, working there, them guys, they would take the tips. A lot of them guys would steal the tips, you know, and what a little snotty thing, a man handed a dollar and he'd stick it in his pocket, you know. He didn't want us to leave though, he wanted us to, I think his name was Demling. What is that, is that Irish or sweet? Demling. Sounds more like Irish, I guess. Yeah, Demling, that was the guy's name. And he didn't want us to leave, he wanted to keep us over there, but the boys all got married, we can't make no money. Yeah. So we left.
What do you think about Bach and all this new junk they play nowadays?

This new stuff is alright, this new stuff is alright. On the synth, the new stuff they got now, they ain't got no, you might say, no foundation. They ain't got no foundation. Everybody's jumping up and out and in and up, you know, and you can't, you can't tell, you can't get the significance of the piece, you know. That's a hard tune. Yeah, you don't know what they're playing, you can't tell what they're playing. There ain't no lead. And the fellow that's playing the lead should be playing the lead. He's jumping from here and different places, you see. And you can't, you can't tell what they're playing. But you get one band that has a good lead, and then them fellas playing that other junk, you know, see. It's better, it's all better, you know. Yeah, we had a nice band.
Yeah, I'd like to hear you with a real good...
I'll wait some days to practice up and get together. Get together.

It wouldn't take you long, I don't believe, to get back in shape as far as the... I don't think so, no. I mean, anybody really knows something, as they say, you never forget it. No, you never forget it. Like they say, for instance, riding a bicycle, if you've never ridden for ten years, you can get on a bicycle. Try to get on a bicycle and go right on. And they say, you can't swim like me, you're like me. But they say, if you once learned to swim when you were a kid, maybe fifty years later, somebody will push you in the water and you'll swim. You go right on, eh? You learn how to do it. And I know with your music, you can pick up that trombone again. It might take you, well, a couple of weeks to get you in there, to get shape, maybe. Yeah, it'd take you in about a couple of weeks, I guess, Mike.

But still, it'd be better than almost anybody can do now. Oh, yeah. I've never heard, I'm sure. Yeah, these fellas are playing now. I don't know. I'm not knocking, I'm not knocking like that. But, I don't know, they don't seem to get the right bass on, you know, on trombone. It seem like they're off some way. It seem like they're way back. And sometimes I pick up, sometime on the radio, hear some fellas playing, and he's alright, but there's a few of them, see? Yeah. And the majority, they look like as many bands as they got, look like they ought to always have good trombone. Yeah, I'd think so. But it's hard to get a good trombone player. Now, Percy Jackson, he's a nice trombone player. Yeah. He plays nice trombone. He took lessons from you, too, here in Chicago. Yeah, he sure did. Uh-huh. Yeah, he did.
There's one other New Orleans tromboneist here, Albert Wynn. Do you know that?
Yeah, he took a couple of lessons. He didn't stay, but he took enough to learn to play pretty good. He plays pretty good.

What's one of them? He's around. He, uh, up in our place where a friend, we have a piano, sort of a studio, not a real big recording studio, but some bands used to come up and rehearse. And about a year ago, he was there with a few people. Oh, yeah? I can't remember who, oh, Jasper Taylor. Yeah, Jasper Taylor, yeah. He was with him. He was with him.
Nice.

And, uh, Albert Wynn played pretty nice, I thought. Yeah. Nice, uh. He doesn't work much. Like I said, there aren't many bands here Chicago that do use a trombone unless they... No, there is a trombone. Oh, no. Just about to. I think we'd better quit. Dave Payton, yes, I heard that Dave Payton died. I knew him. I never heard him play much, but I talked to him a couple of times. He was a good pianist. Nice piano.
He arranged, too.
He's a good arranger, too. Yeah, he's a good arranger. But when did you start arranging music and composing? Mm-hmm. When you got started?

Well, it's around. No, I was in, uh, New Orleans when I started arranging and getting myself set for arranging. And then, uh, after I come here, I just went on arranging, kept it up. After you get a set up, you know, and know just what you're doing and know what to do, you just go right on. You don't have to worry, you see. I didn't graduate in no school, music school, for that, you know.
But I just... No more than a lot of people that do, I know that. Yeah. You have that talent.
Yeah, you see, that's been training. You worked at it yourself, a real experience. Yeah, that's the idea. Yeah. I had to fight myself, but I, I made it.
When did you start teaching? Did you have any pupils in New Orleans?

Well, I had, no, I had more pupils here than I had in New Orleans. I had about, I had about 40. I had about... Really? About 12 white boys from over on the west side. And then I had more, well, more than 40 of us. They'd come every other night. I wasn't doing nothing but teaching them. I didn't have to worry. I was teaching them on different instruments, see. And they'd come in the night. And the only thing about me was, when I was teaching, I give a man too much time. See, I couldn't, I can't get away from that. I'm just taking up in it and I know when you're doing good. I want to see you do good and I'll forget about the time. Some teachers will hold it. A half hour, yeah. Every half hour. You had to go, see. And sometimes, my wife used to tell me, say, my goodness, did you teach a fellow that long? Or that long? You say, well, no, it isn't that. I see them doing good and I just get, you know, in me that I want to see them still do and do better. That's why I hold myself over that way. But as far as teaching, I believe I can learn any of them, anything. If they listen at me and go the way I want them to go, see, it'll be easier for them like this boy there. You should hear him. Is he still around playing here in Chicago? Yeah, he's around now, but he's been kind of sick, see, and he ain't been playing much. They got him off the trumpet for a while, see. He's a young kid. He's about 18 or 19 years old. But he's good. All that drawl was stuck, all that diminishes and stuff like Louis Armstrong play. And he picked that up himself, see. I got him one of those methods we just called, Auburn Method. And got him, he didn't get all the way through it, see. He just got to about a little on the other side of half. That boy was doing things that way. I'll be the best way to instruct a person, take them slow. Let them see slow, let they, they'll work up fast on it, see. Just let them go along slow and go along, make them divide it right. And when you let them loose, they're gone. Go with itself, see. Yeah. Because he got the right way to go, see. A whole lot of fellas, teacher fellas, they don't, can I just give me the money. That's all they want, give me the money. That takes too much interest in my scholars. That's the trouble. My wife used to give me the sins. I'm tired of holding a fella like he's teaching them half an hour. And that clock would be 25 minutes. I wouldn't let them loose some time until they're 25 minutes too. See, well that's that man gaining. I'm cheating myself out of about 15 or 20 minutes, see. Yeah. I could have the other fella there, see. So.
You taught all the different instruments, the instruments, clarinet too? Yeah, clarinet and everything.

Clarinet, violin, and uh. Well you played violin for a while. Yeah, I played a little bit. Did you play much on the others? On the others ones, yeah. Trumpet, yeah. I played trumpet and lots and bass fiddle, bass drum, bass horn. I never, you know, kept them for a regular, but I had to know them. Sure. You know, I had to know them. So. Yeah. That's it. So I just kept on, got them all down, worked out. And I got some good, I put some good bands together. I want to sing about these boys, these young boys. They don't, they don't, they don't stay long enough to learn what they ought to learn. Before, if they learn how to play the blues or something, and get a couple of breaks, and play a couple of diminishes, he's gone. Think they know what they're going to do? Yeah, they think he knows something. See, he's gone. I had a boy by the name of Joe Valadie. He was a nice trumpet player. He went on himself. After he got his 15th lesson, he went on. I couldn't hold him, see, he went on. But he come back, see, and I wouldn't fool with him. I wouldn't, because I knew he would have been too good a trumpet player if he had stayed and took what I wanted to give him. But he got out there too early. Then after he got out there early, the brothers told him, say, you ought to have stayed under that man. You should have went, stayed there and learned something. See, he couldn't read good enough, you know, to stay with them big shots, you know. They told him, say, you should have stayed under the man you was under, and you would have been able to play. And he come back with, I wouldn't fool with him. I told him, I said, Mr. Best, I wouldn't fool with you. I said, because you had a chance to learn trumpet and do what you wanted, put up your own band. If you learn how to play good, I said, you could hire fellas. He said, that's right. He said, I'm sorry. I said, I wouldn't fool with you. Take a lesson today and maybe day after tomorrow or next weekend or something like that.
Just losing time, see. Did you ever work with a whole band, a young band, to try to teach the whole band together?

Yeah, I had a young band, yeah. I had them put them. I had, oh, twenty some odd pieces. I had them together and I put them together. Sometimes I'd take them out of the first grade on the band and all the good ones, I pick them out. The baritone, you're clarinet, you can play in three sharps, two sharps. If a man can play in two sharps, you can take them, you can put them in the band. He'll make out, see. Two sharps or two flats, you can put them in there, he'll make out, see. Then you get them little low grade ones, first grade ones. The boys, they didn't know the instruments, they just know the scales, you know. Well, I wouldn't put them, I wouldn't tell them later on that they'd learn how to play, you know, on a different scale. Then I let them in. Oh, I had a ton. Good band, some halfway bands, some of them wasn't going to like nothing because they, I had a band of, I had a band of ladies. They were good. Really? But the, but the teacher up there, yeah. Well, there's a picture up there. Yeah. Is that the one? Yeah, that's one. That's it, yeah. But that's some of the women, but I wasn't in that, this is another fellow got this, but there's some of the women in there. Oh, some of that. And, uh. Sorry, the brass band? Yeah, it was a brass band. And, uh, I don't know. They was playing and practicing and playing. They could play a number. When I picked them up, see, they was playing already. But there wasn't one of them women who hardly could play a scale. Couldn't play a scale. Played by ear and? Played by, well, they knew the notes, but they, I don't know what, you know, I don't know what you could say about them.
They wouldn't practice that, I guess.

I guess they needed to practice, see, and study. And, uh, they wouldn't study. And whenever they had a job, yeah, women would come out of their homes, man, full of cobweb. They done had it hanging up. Before I forget. But they hear about a job. When they hear about a job, there's those women that's playing. Sure, they got homes, you know, even shine them up. You know how it felt. Yeah.
Before I forget, I want to ask about, in learning trombone, how young can you start?

A real little kid can teach it, could he? Yeah, you can start a little kid. You can start, well, about, say about eight years old. You can start a kid eight years old. And he'll make it. Like the violin.
I started, I played violin myself. I started on three-quarter sizes. Yeah, three-quarters, a little bit.
I got about twelve, I got a bigger one.
Uh-huh. But trombone is only the one size, isn't it?
Yeah, trombone is one size.
Unless he got him one of them sliding corners. Yeah. Louis had one of those on the boat, I got a picture. Baby Dodds and Louis.

Joe Oliver tried to play one too, yeah. He had one. They didn't do no good though. I don't know why, but they couldn't make good on the sliding trumpet. There was one fellow, there was that guy, and he was a white fellow. He was playing the sliding trumpet, and he come through here with his shoulder. That guy could fool that thing. But I guess he must have been the trombone, ex-trombone player. Maybe. Yeah, he must have been. Yeah, he was really good. So the kid could start then at eight years old.
Oh yeah, he would start a kid at eight years old. He couldn't reach down to sixth and seventh position.

No, but as he'd go along, you see, you've got to give him anyhow about a year to get him straightened and teach him that position where that little toe is at and all like that. That's like a little girl playing piano. You can play that piano all over there, and if there's a key out, that girl play that piano and don't, she don't think about that key and play the whole piece. See, that key, you know, if it's out, dead key, you know, she'll play over that dead key. Now I couldn't go there and play it over somebody that plays piano. Couldn't hardly go, because the first thing they'd say, this piano's bad, it's missing keys. I can't play it, see? I can't go there, just go on and play it. Yeah.
He was learning, you know, kids he was learning, but he was doing fine. A lot of those kids are smart, very smart. You just have to take pains with them though.
Well, I was going to ask about those records you made for Jelly Roll Morton, and we played the Tiger Rag and Weary Blues. Can you tell anything about that session, who all was on that?

That's what I want to say. I know some of those fellas, but some of those guys got away from me. There were some of them that left Chicago. I don't know where they went to, but I know they left here, but I do know that Arnett Nelson was with us, because many times Arnett Nelson used to tease Jelly Roll, you know. Jelly Roll had a place down in the loop, you know. And he used to be down there, he wore derby, you know, in long shoes. Them guys draw the picture of Jelly Roll and made him mad. You know Jelly Roll, don't you? I know, yes. Yeah, yeah, yeah. He got mad, guys got sober with him, but he come all right after, he's all right. But this guy, Arnett, myself, and Jelly Roll had two or three fellas there, I didn't know from over on the north side. He lived way over on the, way over on Sedgwick, over there, Harmon Edwards. He lived over on Sedgwick and the fella played bass fiddle. Bass fiddle, what is his name? That's a Burton too. He played with the other role. Burton, I don't know what's his first name. Burton, bass tuba player. He quit playing. Lee Collins. Yeah, and Lee Collins was with us. And let's see who else. Did Lee use the cornet then or trumpet, I guess? Lee played the trumpet. I believe he had a half from a medium side, you might call it a cornet and a medium side.
He played. Remember anything about that, whether those records were made, they were right here in Chicago, wasn't it? Yeah, all the records were made, they were right here in Chicago.

And most of all, outside the door we made in New York with Fatten and the banjo player, we made them, we went to New York and made them. But it wasn't with Jethro then, we made them, not with some of the numbers, we made in New York with Melrose, see? Melrose. Let's see, yeah, Melrose, we made most of, a lot of those numbers with Melrose. I wish I could get a good number and put on the records, you know, to show them trombone and play it hard to play. Yeah, I wish you could too. Yeah. I'm going to get together and practice. I'd like to hear you. I've never heard you in person except for the records. Well sir.
Yeah, I wish you would.
Yeah, I know. Well you'd be just as happy as you would if you were sitting and listening that. I'd do a bit more, you know, just.
Yeah, I know. I can tell from those records, I've heard everybody talk so much about how wonderful you were. Yeah.
I used to get a lot of praise.
Is there anything else you can tell about the Jolly Row, how you liked his piano style, or was he considered about the best pianist?

The best pianist I remember was Weatherford, about the best pianist. I played with him at Rich Carlton, and he was about the best piano player I played with around. I played with Earl Hines a little. I played one or two jobs in Earl Hines. And this Zinke Korn. Oh yeah. I played with him. I heard him. Yeah.
He died not long ago. Yeah, he sure did. He was a nice piano player.
Lily Armstrong, she was nice.
She was here last year. She's back in Paris and, oh she's back in Paris. Yeah. She's back in Rome now with Albert Nicholas. Do you remember Albert Nicholas?
Yeah, yeah. Sure, he's a alto sax guy.
He's a clarinetist too.

Oh yeah, clarinetist, that's right. Played with Oliver. Mm-hmm. Did you ever play with Louis Armstrong? Louis Armstrong, I played with him a while a little bit. He played with us over at the Dream. We had him playing with us there. He played with us a while over there. But I never played regular with Louis. I played more regular with Joe Oliver than I did Louis.
When were you with Oliver?

I was with Oliver about 1922 I think or 20, something like that. Royal Garden? Yeah, we was over there. We used to alternate. We used to shift from the Dreamland to, uh, Dreamland to, uh, Royal Garden. And after Louis, after Joe got here a while, he got with a band. He wasn't with a band when he come here. And he had to send and get the boys with him, see. And then Louis Armstrong was in St. Louis, see. Louis come from St. Louis here. Yeah, he'd been on the boat. Yeah. So, that was our, that was our starts and our beginnings. 된 stuff
